content: Acron, the son of Xenon, was a distinguished Greek physician born in Agrigentum. The exact date of his birth is not known, but he is noted to have been a contemporary of Empedocles, who died around the beginning of the Peloponnesian War. This places Acron's life in the 5th century BC. He later moved from Sicily to Athens, where he established a philosophical school. It is reported that Acron was present in Athens during the great plague of 430 BC. During this time, he is said to have directed the lighting of large fires in the streets to purify the air, which reportedly provided significant relief to many of the afflicted. However, this account is not corroborated by Thucydides. Furthermore, if it is true that Empedocles or Simonides (who died in 467 BC) composed Acron's epitaph, it raises doubts about whether Acron was in Athens during the plague at all. Upon returning to his homeland, Acron requested a plot of land from the senate to construct a family tomb. This request was denied, influenced by Empedocles, who believed that granting such a privilege would undermine the principle of equality he sought to establish in Agrigentum. Acron's epitaph, noted for its intricate wordplay, is considered one of the most elaborate examples of paronomasia and is preserved in Greek to maintain its original linguistic nuances. The second line of the epitaph has been subject to variations, and some attribute the entire epigram to Simonides. Pliny the Elder regarded Acron as the first of the Empiricists. However, this is considered an error, as the Empiric school did not emerge until the 3rd century BC, approximately 200 years after Acron's time. Some scholars suggest that the Empiricists, in an effort to claim greater antiquity than the Dogmatics (founded around 400 BC by Thessalus and Polybus, relatives of Hippocrates), may have retroactively claimed Acron as their founder. None of Acron's works have survived to the present day. Nevertheless, he authored several writings in the Doric dialect on medical and physical topics, the titles of which are preserved in the works of the Suda and Eudocia.
